pinnacle

PIN-uh-kul — think of a mountain's 'pin'-sharp point; the pinnacle is the very top. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Pinnacle is the most successful point of something; the highest peak.

Winning the Nobel Prize marked the absolute pinnacle of the scientist's forty-year career.

Worked Example

A young violinist practices for fifteen years, wins a string of regional competitions, and is finally invited to perform as a soloist with the world's most famous orchestra in front of a sold-out concert hall.

That final, career-defining moment -- the highest point everything else was building toward -- is exactly what pinnacle means. Unlike 'goal,' which is just something aimed for, pinnacle specifically means the very peak of achievement.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

summit: A summit is the literal topmost point of a mountain, reached by climbing -- climbers touch the summit, take a photograph, and descend. Pinnacle long ago moved into figurative territory: the pinnacle of a career or a civilization is an achievement, not a rock. A summit is climbed; a pinnacle is earned.

crowning achievement: A crowning achievement is the single accomplishment itself -- the prize, the record, the masterpiece -- that tops everything else a person has done. Pinnacle names the position rather than the deed: the highest point of the career or era that such an achievement marks.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

nadir: the lowest point of something

low point: the worst or least successful moment

Where it sits · how absolute the high point is — peak → pinnacle → zenith

peak vs. pinnacle: Peak is a more everyday, general word than pinnacle -- something can peak often (like traffic or temperature), while pinnacle is reserved for a rare, career-defining high point.

zenith vs. pinnacle: Zenith can feel even more formal and absolute than pinnacle: pinnacle suggests the top of a climb, but zenith suggests the single highest point possible, with nothing above it.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — pinn-

root — pinn-: point, peak, feather (Latin (pinna))

suffix — -acle

suffix — -acle: small, diminutive (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin pinna meant 'point, feather, wing-tip' -- something that comes to a sharp end. A pinnacle, at its root, is a small sharp peak, which is why the word came to mean the very highest point of anything.

Use the root in a new word: pinnate

Use the root in a new word: pinnate: The fern's pinnate leaves fanned out like feathers along a central stem.
